g.text: This capture covers 4 seconds: 156 packets (24.6 KB) from 10 devices on the local network talking to 5
outside addresses. Most of it was unencrypted web traffic (HTTP, 32%) and devices announcing themselves
(mDNS/SSDP, 21%). 16 things deserve a closer look; the most serious is port scan from 10.0.0.66. 3 devices
announced themselves on the local network (Living Room (Apple TV 4K 3rd gen), Kitchen speaker (Google Nest
Mini), Samsung smart TV or streaming device). That chatter is normal.
One host probed many ports in a short window.
FIN, PSH and URG set together ('lit up like a Christmas tree') is a stealth scanning technique.
A TCP packet with no flags set has no legitimate use.
An IP address suddenly claimed a different MAC address.
A request tried to climb out of the web root with ../ to read system files.
Traffic used a port associated with backdoors, botnet C2 or remote-access services.
RC4, DES/3DES, NULL and EXPORT ciphers can be broken or offer no encryption at all.
The server presented a certificate past its expiry date.
… and 9 more kinds of warning (see the alerts view)
Looked up 5 names: login.paypa1-secure.com, api.example.com, ocis2jhtlgmxgedn73u55xtplpft7v4seh2kvj…
Tried 19 different services on 10.0.0.23: FTP, SSH, TELNET, SMTP and 15 more
Announced itself as an Apple TV 4K 3rd gen running tvOS 26.6, offering AirPlay, Apple device li…
Announced itself as a Google Nest Mini, offering Google Cast
Looked for AirPlay screens (Apple TVs, smart TVs), Chromecasts and Google Cast speakers and 2 more …
Samsung smart TV or streaming device
Announced itself as a Samsung smart TV or streaming device, offering casting (DIAL)
15 packets were background chatter from devices finding each other (announcements, searches and ARP), grouped
into the lines above. Devices on a home or office network constantly announce what they are and look for each
other (mDNS/Bonjour, SSDP/UPnP, ARP). It is normal and usually not worth worrying about.
